newsitem.title: GERMANY: Papers say Bonn to raise VAT to help fund reform.
newsitem.headline: Papers say Bonn to raise VAT to help fund reform.

text.p: A German newspaper reported on Sunday that the ruling coalition has decided to raise value-added tax (VAT) by two percentage points to help finance a broad tax reform in 1999.
Bonn officials would not confirm the unsourced report in Bild am Sonntag.
Separately, Focus magazine reported that the government had dropped controversial plans to tax capital gains from share transactions more heavily.
Focus said the government would keep the current system under which gains are tax-exempt provided that investors wait six months before realising them.
A spokeswoman for the finance ministry contacted by Reuters said she could not confirm that a decision had been reached to raise VAT by two percentage points.

She said a tax policy working group chaired by finance minister Theo Waigel was scheduled to hold its final meeting on Wednesday. The results of the months-long discussions will be presented to the coalition parties on Thursday.

The report in Bild am Sonntag said Waigel had confirmed VAT would be raised and quoted him as saying the reduced VAT rate on products like food, newspapers and books would remain unchanged at seven percent.

Bonn is widely expected to raise VAT to help finance a tax reform with which Waigel aims to lighten the burden on German taxpayers by a net 30 billion marks ($18 billion) to help boost jobs and investment in the cost-laden economy.
Bild am Sonntag quoted Waigel as saying: "With a value-added-tax rise we will maintain the reduced VAT rate at seven percent."
"That means the impact for low earners, pensioners or large families will be very acceptable socially."
Medical services and tickets for museums, theatres and wildlife parks will remain exempt from VAT, the paper said.
News magazine "Der Spiegel" reported that the working group had agreed to reduce the lowest income tax rate to 19.5 percent from 25.9 percent.
Sources close to the ruling coalition have already said that the top tax rate wil be cut to 39 percent from 53 percent.
